title: API Versioning
description: Learn how to evolve your Next.js API without breaking existing clients using URL paths, headers, and content negotiation.

data.text: APIs change. Fields get renamed, responses get restructured, and endpoints get replaced. Versioning gives you a safe path to ship improvements while keeping older clients working.

Imagine you ship a mobile app that calls your API. If you change the response shape without warning, the app breaks for every user until they update. Versioning lets you deploy changes and give clients time to migrate.

items: Support old and new clients during migration
Avoid emergency rollbacks after breaking changes
Document which versions are active and deprecated
Give teams confidence to refactor internals

data.text: The most common and clearest approach is to put the version in the URL. `/api/v1/posts` and `/api/v2/posts` are explicit, easy to test, and obvious to clients. Next.js Route Handlers make this simple with nested folders.

data.title: URL versioned Route Handlers

data.text: Some teams prefer keeping URLs clean and passing the version in a custom header like `API-Version: 2` or through the `Accept` header. This keeps the path stable but is less visible in browser history and logs.

data.title: Branching by Accept header
Start With URL Versioning
data.text: URL path versioning is the easiest to debug, test, and document. You can migrate to header versioning later if you really need cleaner URLs, but most teams never outgrow paths.
Versioning only works if you eventually retire old versions. Announce deprecations in response headers and documentation, give clients a runway to migrate, then delete the old endpoint.

data.title: Adding deprecation headers
Key Takeaways
items: URL path versioning (`/api/v1/...`) is the simplest and most explicit
Header versioning keeps URLs clean but is harder to debug
Deprecate old versions with `Sunset` and `Link` headers
Give clients advance notice and a clear migration path
